a01.title: An LLM gateway for your company
a01.prompt: Every team calls LLM APIs directly with their own keys. Design one gateway: 40 services, 2 million requests a day, peak 5x average, average 1,500 input and 300 output tokens. Needs: per-team budgets, model routing (small vs large), prompt caching, retries, logging of cost per request, and no keys in services.
a01.deliverable: A one-page design: diagram (clients → gateway → providers), the request path, how routing and budgets work, a cost estimate per day at two model prices, and two trade-offs.

a02.title: An evaluation platform for LLM features
a02.prompt: Ten product teams ship prompts and agents. Design a platform that stores eval sets, runs them on every prompt or model change in CI, supports code graders and calibrated model judges, and blocks releases that regress. 50 suites × 200 cases, run on every pull request.
a02.deliverable: Diagram, data model (suite, case, run, score), the CI flow, how judges are calibrated, cost per full run, and what you would cut for version 1.

a03.title: A platform for autonomous data agents
a03.prompt: Agents will triage pipeline failures, answer data questions and propose dbt fixes for 300 data users. Design the runtime: MCP tool servers, permissions, approval gates, budgets, traces and evaluation. Agents must never write to production without approval.
a03.deliverable: Diagram, permission model per tool, the approval flow, what is logged and for how long, how you measure success, and the riskiest failure mode with its mitigation.

s00.title: Your study system as a data product
s00.prompt: Warm-up: design how this app could store your progress for 3 devices with offline use and sync once a day.
s00.deliverable: Five boxes, where state lives, and one conflict case with how you resolve it.

s01.title: Rides analytics from scratch
s01.prompt: A ride-hailing company has 2 million trips a day in 6 cities. Product wants hourly completed trips per city with at most 1 hour delay. Design ingestion, storage, processing, serving and orchestration.
s01.deliverable: Back-of-envelope (events/s, GB/day), a five-box diagram, where each tool sits, and a decision record for Kafka vs direct writes.

s02.title: A lake that survives growth
s02.prompt: Trips grow 10x to 20 million a day. Queries over 2 years of data take minutes and small files keep appearing. Design the table layout and maintenance.
s02.deliverable: Partitioning and sort choices with reasons, file size targets, compaction and snapshot expiry schedule, and before/after query cost estimate.

s03.title: Spark at 20x scale
s03.prompt: The daily Silver job grows from 30 GB to 600 GB and one city is 40% of the data. Design cluster sizing and the job so it finishes within 1 hour.
s03.deliverable: Executor sizing maths, how you handle skew, shuffle partitions, and what you monitor in the Spark UI.

s04.title: A warehouse people trust
s04.prompt: Finance and product disagree on "revenue". Design the dimensional model and the semantic layer so both get the same number.
s04.deliverable: Fact and dimension tables with grain, SCD choices, metric definitions, tests, and ownership.

s05.title: Surge pricing in real time
s05.prompt: Compute supply and demand per city zone every 30 seconds from 50,000 events per second, with late events up to 2 minutes.
s05.deliverable: Streaming topology, windowing and watermarks, state size estimate, exactly-once sink, and what happens when the job restarts.

s06.title: Source of truth with CDC
s06.prompt: Orders live in Postgres (5,000 writes/s). Analytics needs every change in the lakehouse within 5 minutes, including deletes.
s06.deliverable: CDC pipeline, ordering and deduplication, how deletes and schema changes flow, and the reconciliation check.

s07.title: Move it to AWS for under $3,000 a month
s07.prompt: Lift the platform to AWS. Budget $3,000/month. Design services, IAM, networking and cost controls.
s07.deliverable: Service map, IAM roles per job, a monthly cost table, and three cost guardrails.

s08.title: Two engines, one set of tables
s08.prompt: Data science uses Databricks, analytics uses Snowflake. Design storage and governance so both read the same tables without copies.
s08.deliverable: Table format and catalog choice, access control model, lineage, and the interop trade-offs.

s09.title: Reliability you can measure
s09.prompt: The CEO dashboard was wrong three times last quarter. Design SLOs, data contracts, tests and on-call for the top 20 tables.
s09.deliverable: SLO definitions, contract format, test layers, alert routing, and the incident process.

s10.title: A full design round (45 minutes)
s10.prompt: Design a real-time driver earnings service: 1 million drivers check earnings 5 times a day; numbers must match payouts.
s10.deliverable: Follow the six steps: requirements, estimate, high-level design, deep dive, trade-offs, wrap-up.

s11.title: In front of the customer
s11.prompt: A logistics customer wants "AI insights on delays" in 6 weeks. Run discovery and design the smallest useful first release.
s11.deliverable: Ten discovery questions, a metric tree, a v1 scope, and a one-page proposal with risks.

s12.title: Architecture review board
s12.prompt: Present your platform to a review board. Defend three decisions and answer "what breaks at 10x?".
s12.deliverable: C4 context and container diagrams, three ADRs, and a 10x risk list.

m01.title: Model a ride-hailing marketplace where drivers can also be riders
m01.prompt: Lyft-style case: one person can be a rider, a driver, or both. Model people, vehicles, trips, ratings and city changes so that analysts can answer "revenue by the driver's city at trip time" and "how many drivers also ride".
m01.deliverable: A star schema sketch: the trip fact with its grain stated, each dimension with its SCD type and why, how one person is both rider and driver (role-playing dimension), and one as-of join written out.

m02.title: Facts for a card ledger with holds and disputes
m02.prompt: Capital One-style case: card authorisations place holds, settlements post later (sometimes for a different amount), and disputes can reverse a charge weeks later. Finance needs daily balances; risk needs the life of every transaction.
m02.deliverable: Name each fact table, its type (transaction, periodic snapshot, accumulating snapshot) and grain; which measures are additive, semi-additive or not; how reversals are recorded without updating history; and how late settlements are handled.

m03.title: Pick the model for every layer of the platform
m03.prompt: For the Meridian platform, choose the data model for each stage: raw events from apps and Postgres CDC, the cleaned layer, the business layer for Finance and Ops, a real-time driver feature for surge pricing, and a semantic layer an LLM can query safely.
m03.deliverable: A one-page table: stage, model (event log, 3NF or Data Vault, star schema or OBT, cumulative, key-value or feature store, semantic layer), why, the anti-pattern you avoid, and how write-audit-publish gates each step.

j01.title: Run Spark and Flink on Kubernetes for twenty teams
j01.prompt: Meridian wants one shared platform where twenty teams run Spark batch jobs and Flink streaming jobs on Kubernetes instead of each team owning a cluster. Some jobs are business-critical, most are ad hoc, and costs must be charged back to teams.
j01.deliverable: A one-page design: namespaces and quotas per team, requests and limits, priority classes for critical jobs, the operators you use, how shuffle and checkpoints are stored, autoscaling, how a team submits a job (the paved path), observability, and how cost is attributed.

r01.title: Migrate the Hive warehouse to Iceberg without downtime
r01.prompt: Meridian has 400 Hive tables, 1,200 Airflow tasks and 30 dashboards on the old warehouse. Leadership wants everything on Iceberg within two quarters, with no broken dashboards and no wrong numbers in Finance reports.
r01.deliverable: A design doc: goals and non-goals, inventory and ordering (by risk and dependency), dual-run and reconciliation, cutover and rollback per table, how consumers are moved and old tables deprecated, the cost of running both, milestones, and the three biggest risks with mitigations.

d01.title: A trip store that survives a lost data centre
d01.prompt: Meridian needs an operational store for live trips: 50,000 writes a second at peak, riders and drivers read their own trip state constantly, and the service must keep working if one of three data centres goes down.
d01.deliverable: The storage engine and why (B-tree or LSM), the partition key and how hot cities are handled, replication factor and R/W quorum settings, the read-your-writes guarantee, what happens during a data-centre outage (CAP choice), and how the analytics copy is fed (CDC) without double counting.

a04.title: Ask-your-data for the operations team
a04.prompt: Ops leads ask 200 questions a week about trips, drivers and cancellations, and wait two days for an analyst. Design an assistant that answers from the warehouse: 300 tables, a semantic layer with 40 metrics, PII in the riders table, answers in under 10 seconds.
a04.deliverable: A one-page design: the six layers, which questions go to metrics and which to guarded SQL, the MCP tools and their limits, the eval set and the release rule, and a monthly cost estimate.

a05.title: A runbook assistant that stays fresh
a05.prompt: On-call engineers search 8,000 runbook pages and 50,000 past incident notes. Pages change daily and some are deleted. Design retrieval with citations, access by team, and an index that is never more than 15 minutes behind the wiki.
a05.deliverable: Ingest and query paths in boxes, the chunk schema with metadata, how changes and deletes reach the index, where vectors live and why, and the retrieval eval with its target.

o01.title: Move a central data team to domain-owned data products
o01.prompt: A marketplace has 600 engineers, 14 product domains and one central data team of 45 that owns 3,000 warehouse tables. The team's backlog is five months; 40% of incidents come from upstream schema changes nobody announced; three dashboards show three different numbers for active sellers. Leadership wants domains to own their data within 18 months, at no more than 10% higher data spend.
o01.deliverable: A two-page plan: which domains move first and why, what the self-serve platform must offer before they do (with the order you build it), the contract and SLO each product must have, the five global governance rules enforced in code, which products stay central, how you dual-run and retire the old tables, the metrics you report each quarter, and two risks with what you will do about them.

o02.title: A golden path for new data products
o02.prompt: A company of 300 engineers has 25 domain teams publishing data products. Starting a new batch product takes six weeks: teams copy an old repository, ask the platform team for a warehouse schema, an Airflow connection, access roles and alerts by ticket, and half of them skip tests. Design the golden path that gets a new product to its first production run in one day.
o02.deliverable: A two-page design: the journey today versus with the path, the scaffolder's questions, what the template creates and which parts come from shared workflows, the defaults, the guardrails in CI with the waiver rule, how templates are versioned and upgraded, how it appears in the developer portal, the four numbers you will track, and two risks.

a06.title: From pilot to 200,000 conversations a day
a06.prompt: A customer-support assistant works well in a pilot with 500 users. The company wants it for every customer: 200,000 conversations a day, peak 4x average, answers grounded in 30,000 help articles, a budget of $1,000 a day, and a p95 time to first token under one second. Last week a model update made refund answers worse and nobody noticed for six days. Design how it runs in production.
a06.deliverable: A two-page design: the request path with a p95 latency budget per step, the cost per request and per day with the two levers that bring it under budget (and their risks), the gateway rules it relies on, the golden set and regression gate every prompt or model change must pass, online checks on live traffic (including a judge you have checked against people), the trace each request writes and the three alerts you would set, and how a model update is rolled out.

o03.title: Govern a fintech lakehouse
o03.prompt: A payments company keeps 4 PB in an Iceberg lakehouse read by Spark, Trino and a warehouse, by 1,500 people in 12 countries. Card numbers, emails and national ids sit in raw and silver tables; access is 900 roles granted by ticket; erasure requests take six weeks and nobody is sure old snapshots are cleaned; regulators want proof of who saw customer data. Design the governance that fixes this in two quarters.
o03.deliverable: A two-page design: how personal data is found and tagged (declared, detected, reviewed), the access model (roles versus tag and attribute policies, row and column rules, expiry and reviews) enforced in every engine, which data is masked, tokenised or pseudonymised and why, how lineage is collected and used, the retention classes and the erasure flow with legal holds and snapshot expiry, the audit evidence, the order you deliver it in, and two risks.

o04.title: Run a data platform team as a product
o04.prompt: A data platform team of 12 serves 40 domain teams on a lakehouse that costs 4 million a year. There is no roadmap (the loudest request wins), incidents happen every week, 35% of spend has no team tag, a satisfaction survey scored 5 out of 10, and three teams have started building their own stacks. The new CTO wants a plan within a month and results within two quarters.
o04.deliverable: A two-page plan: the users and their top journeys, the platform's SLIs and SLOs with the error budget policy and burn-rate alerts, the on-call and incident changes, the showback model (tags, shared costs, unit costs) and when to move to chargeback, the intake and scoring for the roadmap with the capacity split, the five numbers you report monthly, what you will stop doing, and two risks.

o05.title: The data foundation blueprint for a ride and delivery marketplace
o05.prompt: A ride and delivery marketplace in 9 countries has 40 million customers, 25 Postgres databases behind its apps, 1.5 billion product events a day (peak 4x on Friday evenings and launches), 30 SaaS sources, 600 analysts and 80 ML models. Today there are three warehouses, nightly dumps, no catalog, revenue that finance and product report differently, new datasets that take six weeks, and data spend growing 45% a year with nobody owning it. EU and Indian customer data must stay in region. The data team is 35 engineers. Write the blueprint for the next three years.
o05.deliverable: The ten-part blueprint (about six pages): the business and its numbers with the arithmetic; five to seven principles; the architecture layer by layer with one rejected alternative each; data products and owners; golden paths; governance with residency; the platform's SLOs; capacity and cost per year and per unit with a three-year comparison of two options; the first 90 days, the year and the migration from the three warehouses; and the top risks with early warning numbers. Pass the simulator's foundation challenge and rehearse the 10-minute review.
